name: Corsage Green
lede: Corsage Green is a light, muted green from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the pinned flower arrangement though the dictionary never says which bloom it had in mind.

sections.title: Named for a flower, unspecified
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul list Corsage Green at #5F9C82 on plate 28, row G, column 6 of their 1930 dictionary, dating its first recorded use to 1927 [1]. The ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 files the same swatch as "light green" [1]. A corsage is a small bouquet pinned to clothing, but which flower or greenery gave the color its name is undocumented in the 29 books behind our concordance [1].

In our color graph the nearest named neighbor is [[bouquet-green|Bouquet Green]], 3.8 units away, a fitting companion given the shared floral naming [1]. A little further, at 5.2 units, is [[motmot-green|Motmot Green]] [1]. The Munsell notation is 6.3G 5.9/4.6, and the swatch sits with our [[green|green]] family; its de2000 distance from a teal reading would place it near [[teal|teal]] as well [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 0.17% of 23,781 paintings, 41 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 19 [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.5% of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 3.9 times the rate its museums would predict [2]. Within a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 47% of its 19 appearances [2]. It is most over-represented in France, 3.1 times the expected rate, 11 of 3,443 French paintings in the archive [2]. The earliest match dates to 1514, by Juan de Flandes, 416 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name, a floor rather than a first [2].
